question_upd: What is the most appropriate course of action after a diagnostic laparoscopy reveals a blind-ending vessel in a 4-year-old boy with absence of the right testis?
exp_upd:
Cryptorchidism is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract. It refers to the condition where one or both testes fail to descend into the scrotum, resulting in a hidden testis. In some cases, a testis may be absent due to agenesis or atrophy, which can occur as a result of intrauterine vascular compromise, also known as the "vanishing testis syndrome." Bilaterally absent testes is a rare condition known as anorchia, which affects approximately 10% of cases. More commonly, one testis is affected, with the right side being more prone to this condition.

Undescended testes can lead to several complications. Torsion, or twisting, of the testis can occur in cases of incomplete testicular descent. Bilateral undescended testes can result in sterility, particularly in cases where the testes are located intra-abdominally. Incomplete testicular descent also increases the risk of malignant disease, although the risk may be diminished by orchidopexy, a surgical procedure to bring the testes into the scrotum.

In some cases, atrophy of an inguinal testis may occur before puberty, possibly due to recurrent minor trauma. In patients with a unilateral nonpalpable testis, a descended testis that is larger than expected may suggest an atrophic undescended testis. Confirmation typically requires surgical intervention, such as diagnostic laparoscopy, to seek an intra-abdominal testis or confirm testicular agenesis. In some cases, scrotal or inguinal exploration may be necessary if a testicular remnant is suspected distal to the internal inguinal ring.

question: 3.5 kg term male baby, born of uncomplicated pregnancy, developed, respiratory distress at birth, not responded to surfactant, ECHO finding revealed nothing abnormal, X–ray showed ground glass appearance and culture negative. Apgars 4 and 5 at 1 and 5 minutes. History of one month female sibling died before. What is the diagnosis ?
exp:
"Respiratory distress in an infant along with a positive family history of similarly affected newborn infants strongly suggests, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis".
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis 

Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is a disorder characterized by the intraalveolar accumulation of pulmonary surfactant.
Two clinically distinct forms of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis are seen -


Fatal form                                -->          Presenting shortly after birth (congenital PAP)

u Gradually progressive form -->           Presenting in older infants and children
Pathology

Although the mechanisms that lead to alveolar proteinosis are undefined, histological findings suggests that they result in a disruption of pulmonary surfactant metabolism.
The main surface tension lowering agent in surfactant is phospholipids le. primary dipalmitol phosphatidyl choline.
However DPCC needs surfactant protein (in endogenous and natural surfactants) for efficient dispersion which enables the formation of a phospholipid monolayer on the alveolar surface.
There are two surfactant proteins present in the body i.e., protein A and protein B.
In pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, there is absence of protein B.
In the absence of protein B, the rapid spread and absorption of the phospholipid (DPCC) does not take place so they cannot form a phospholipid monolayer on the alveolar surface.
This in turn leads to failure of expansion of alveoli leading to poor cardiorespiratory adaptation at birth.

Clinical manifestation -

This disorder is immediately apparent in the newborn period and rapidly leads to respiratory failure.
Congenital pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is clinically and radiographically indistinguishable from more common disorders of the newborn that lead to respiratory failure including pneumonia, generalized bacterial infection, respiratory distress syndrome and total anomalous pulmonary venous return with obstruction.

Diagnosis

Histopathological examination of lung biopsy specimen is the gold standard for diagnosis.
On histopathological examination distal air spaces are filled with a granular, eosinophillic material that stains

positively with periodic - acid schiff reagent and is diastase resistant.
Treatment

Untreated, alveolar proteinosis in newborns is rapidly fatal and no successful medical therapy has been developed.
Repeated bronchoalveolar lavage is a temporizing measure.
Lung transplantation is the only therapeutic option but its use is limited by concerns about disease recurrence.

exp_upd:
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is a disorder characterized by the intraalveolar accumulation of pulmonary surfactant. Two clinically distinct forms of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis are seen: the fatal form, which presents shortly after birth (congenital PAP), and the gradually progressive form, which presents in older infants and children.

The mechanisms that lead to alveolar proteinosis are undefined, but histological findings suggest that they result in a disruption of pulmonary surfactant metabolism. The main surface tension-lowering agent in surfactant is phospholipids, specifically primary dipalmitol phosphatidyl choline (DPCC). However, DPCC needs surfactant protein (in endogenous and natural surfactants) for efficient dispersion, which enables the formation of a phospholipid monolayer on the alveolar surface. There are two surfactant proteins present in the body: protein A and protein B. In pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, there is an absence of protein B. In the absence of protein B, the rapid spread and absorption of the phospholipid (DPCC) do not take place, and they cannot form a phospholipid monolayer on the alveolar surface. This, in turn, leads to failure of alveoli expansion, resulting in poor cardiorespiratory adaptation at birth.

The disorder is immediately apparent in the newborn period and rapidly leads to respiratory failure. Congenital pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is clinically and radiographically indistinguishable from more common disorders of the newborn that lead to respiratory failure, including pneumonia, generalized bacterial infection, respiratory distress syndrome, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return with obstruction.

The gold standard for diagnosis is histopathological examination of a lung biopsy specimen. On histopathological examination, distal air spaces are filled with a granular, eosinophillic material that stains positively with periodic-acid Schiff reagent and is diastase resistant.

Untreated, alveolar proteinosis in newborns is rapidly fatal, and no successful medical therapy has been developed. Repeated bronchoalveolar lavage is a temporizing measure, and lung transplantation is the only therapeutic option, although its use is limited by concerns about disease recurrence.

HYPERPARATHYROIDISM May be primary (due to adenoma or hyperplasia), secondary (due to persistent hypocalcemia) or tertiary (when secondary hyperplasia leads to autonomous overactivity). Fig. X-ray hand--hyperparathyroidism Fig. Brown tumor Figs. A and B: (A) Lamina dura and (B) Resorption of lamina dura Salt pepper skull Parathyroid adenoma Most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism. Presents with subperiosteal resorption, and replacement of endosteal cavitation marrow by vascular granulation and fibrous tissue (osteitis fibrosa cystica). Classical and pathognomic feature of hyperparathyroidism is subperiosteal coical resorption of middle phalanges on radial aspect Clinical features- Abdominal groans (dyspepsia), psychic moans, renal stones and weak bones (Groans, moans, stones and Bones). question_upd: Which investigation can confirm the diagnosis of a patient with pain and swelling in the thigh, multiple lytic lesions in the distal femur on X-ray, and homogenous serosanguinous fluid with RBCs in the aspirate?
exp_upd:
Hyperparathyroidism is a condition characterized by the presence of a blood-filled bone tumor. This condition can be primary, secondary, or tertiary in nature. Primary hyperparathyroidism is caused by an adenoma or hyperplasia, while secondary hyperparathyroidism is caused by persistent hypocalcemia. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism occurs when secondary hyperplasia leads to autonomous overactivity.

The condition is often associated with characteristic radiological features, including subperiosteal resorption and replacement of endosteal cavitation marrow by vascular granulation and fibrous tissue (osteitis fibrosa cystica). The subperiosteal coical resorption of middle phalanges on the radial aspect is a classical and pathognomic feature of hyperparathyroidism.

Clinical features of the condition include abdominal groans (dyspepsia), psychic moans, renal stones, and weak bones (Groans, moans, stones, and Bones). Laboratory tests reveal elevated levels of parathyroid hormone and serum alkaline phosphate, as well as high calcium and low serum phosphate levels.

question: All of the following are suggestive of domestic violence in a child except:
exp: Ans: A. Wormian bones(Ref: Reddy 34/e p417; Parikh 6/e p4. 187).Wormian bones are seen in Osteogenesis imperfecta and not child abuse.Wormian bones, also known as intrasutural bones or sutural bones, are extra bone pieces that can occur within a suture (joint) in the skull. These are irregular isolated bones that can appear in addition to the usual centres of ossification of the skull and, although unusual, are not rare'Battered baby' syndrome:Suspected due to severe & varied changes in metaphyses, periosteal new bone formation or epiphyseal separation.Also referred as "Caffey's Syndrome/Infantile Whiplash Syndrome".Injuries Type & Pattern:Arms & legs:Move about in a whiplash movement resulting in typical 'corner'or 'bucket-handle'-fractures in metaphyseal region.Classical metaphyseal corner or bucket handle fracture" - Viually pathognomonic for abuse.Fractures of acromion, sternum & spinous processes - High specificity for abuse.
opb: Microfractures in the sub-ep physeal region
question_upd: Which of the following is not a suggestive finding of domestic violence in a child?
exp_upd:
Wormian bones, also known as intrasutural bones or sutural bones, are extra bone pieces that can occur within a suture (joint) in the skull. These are irregular isolated bones that can appear in addition to the usual centers of ossification of the skull and, although unusual, are not rare. They are sometimes seen in individuals with osteogenesis imperfecta, a genetic disorder that affects bone development.

In contrast, "battered baby" syndrome, also known as Caffey's Syndrome or Infantile Whiplash Syndrome, is a condition characterized by severe and varied changes in the metaphyses (growth plates) of long bones, periosteal new bone formation, or epiphyseal separation. This condition is often associated with injuries that occur in a whiplash motion, resulting in characteristic "corner" or "bucket-handle" fractures in the metaphyseal region. Fractures of the acromion, sternum, and spinous processes can also be indicative of abuse.

question: All are structures lying deep to the hyoglossus muscle except:
exp:
The hyoglossus, a quadrilateral sheet of muscle, is the key muscle of the suprahyoid region because it serves as a landmark for neighboring structures in the region. 
Superficial relations: 

Hypoglossal nerve, crosses the lower part of muscle from behind forwards.
Lingual nerve, crosses the upper part of muscle from behind forwards.
Deep part of the submandibular gland and submandibular duct. The gland lies in the middle of hyoglossus muscle and the duct lies between the gland and the muscle.
Submandibular ganglion lies between the lingual nerve and deep part of the submandibular gland.
Styloglossus muscle—interdigitates with hyoglossus.
Mylohyoid muscle overlaps the hyoglossus anterosuperiorly.

Deep relations: 

Inferior longitudinal muscle of tongue.
Genioglossus muscle anteriorly.
Middle constrictor of pharynx posteriorly.
Glossopharyngeal nerve.
Stylohyoid ligament.
Lingual artery.

Structures passing deep to posterior border of hyoglossus:

Glossopharyngeal nerve.
Stylohyoid ligament.
Lingual artery.
question_upd: Which of the following structures lies superficial to the hyoglossus muscle?
exp_upd:
The hyoglossus is a quadrilateral sheet of muscle that serves as a landmark for neighboring structures in the suprahyoid region. This muscle has several superficial relations, including the hypoglossal nerve, which crosses the lower part of the muscle from behind forwards, and the lingual nerve, which crosses the upper part of the muscle from behind forwards. The deep part of the submandibular gland and submandibular duct are also situated in relation to the hyoglossus, with the gland lying in the middle of the muscle and the duct lying between the gland and the muscle. Additionally, the submandibular ganglion is located between the lingual nerve and the deep part of the submandibular gland.

The hyoglossus also has deep relations, including the inferior longitudinal muscle of the tongue, the genioglossus muscle, the middle constrictor of the pharynx, the glossopharyngeal nerve, the stylohyoid ligament, and the lingual artery. The posterior border of the hyoglossus is crossed by several structures, including the glossopharyngeal nerve, the stylohyoid ligament, and the lingual artery.

question: The order of caries susceptibility of primary teeth is:
exp:
Caries susceptibility of primary teeth (in descending order)
2nd molar > 1st molar > canine > lateral incisor > central incisor
Caries susceptibility of permanent teeth (in descending order)
1st molar > 2nd molar > Max. 2nd PM > Max. 1st PM & Mand. 2nd PM > Max. central & lateral incisor > Max. canine & Mand. 1st PM > Mand. Central & lateral incisor > Mand. canine
Surfaces involved in descending order (in primary teeth)

question_upd: What is the correct order of caries susceptibility for primary teeth?
exp_upd:
The susceptibility of teeth to caries (tooth decay) varies depending on the type of tooth and its location. In primary teeth, the 2nd molar is most susceptible to caries, followed by the 1st molar, canine, lateral incisor, and central incisor, in that order.

In permanent teeth, the 1st molar is most susceptible to caries, followed by the 2nd molar, maxillary 2nd premolar, maxillary 1st premolar and mandibular 2nd premolar, maxillary central and lateral incisors, maxillary canine and mandibular 1st premolar, and mandibular central and lateral incisors, and mandibular canine, in that order.

The surfaces of primary teeth most commonly affected by caries are the occlusal surface, followed by the molar interproximal surfaces, and then the incisor interproximal surfaces. Notably, the proximal surfaces are more frequently affected in first than in second primary molars.

question: The prevalence of disease in a population is expected to be 50%. An investigator is interested in the range of 45 to 55% with 95% confidence. The minimum sample size required for the study is:
exp: Answer- D (400)In this question, use Standard Error of propoions.The 95% confidence limits for a propoion are p +- 1.96 s.e.p, where s.e.p is the standard error of a propoion.p = sample propoion = propoion of diseased persons = 0.5 q = 1-p = 0.5 s.e.p .NI(p x q / n) Now here, the range of propoions with 95% confidence is mentioned as? 45-55%Hence, 2 s.e.p = 0.55-0.50 = 0.05 s.e.p = 0.0250.025= J(pxq/n)n = 400Thus, the sample size required will be 400.
question_upd: What is the minimum sample size required to estimate the prevalence of disease in a population with a margin of error between 45% and 55%, and with 95% confidence?
exp_upd:
The 95% confidence limits for a proportion are calculated using the standard error of a proportion (SEP). The formula is p ± 1.96 × SEP, where p is the sample proportion, or the proportion of diseased persons. In this case, p = 0.5, and q = 1 - p = 0.5. The standard error of the proportion (SEP) is calculated as √(p × q / n), where n is the sample size.

The range of proportions with 95% confidence is 45-55%. To find the standard error of the proportion, we subtract p from the upper limit and add p to the lower limit, which gives us 0.05. Since 1.96 × SEP = 0.05, we can calculate SEP as 0.025. Finally, substituting this value into the formula for SEP, we get n = 400.

Solitary bone cyst, also known as unicameral bone cyst, is a common diagnosis in children and adolescents, primarily affecting individuals between 5-15 years old. Males are more commonly affected than females. The most common site of occurrence is in the proximal humerus (50-60%), followed by the femur (25-30%).

This condition is characterized by a centrally radiolucent lesion on the metaphyseal side of the growth plate of a long bone. The cyst is not lined by endothelial cells but rather by fibrous tissue and blood vessels, making it a non-true cyst. The clinical features of solitary bone cyst are often asymptomatic, unless the cyst presents as a fracture.

Radiological investigations can confirm the diagnosis, showing a centrally radiolucent lesion on the metaphyseal side of the growth plate of a long bone. The cortex is thinned but intact, and the "fallen fragment sign" may indicate that the lesion is fluid-filled rather than solid. In unusual locations, such as the pelvis, MRI or CT scans may be necessary to document the extent of the lesion and its cystic nature. MRI can also help distinguish solitary bone cyst from other conditions, such as aneurysmal bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and fibrous dysplasia.

Treatment options for solitary bone cyst include curettage, methylprednisolone acetate injection into the lesion, radiographic contrast injection into the lesion, and intralesional injection of sclerosing agents.

exp_upd: The McNaughten rule posits that an individual is not criminally responsible for their actions if they are mentally unsound and incapable of understanding the nature of the act. Durham's rule states that an unlawful act is a direct result of mental disease or mental defect. The irresistible impulse test, meanwhile, holds that even if an individual recognizes the nature and quality of the act as wrong, they may still be excused from criminal responsibility if their free will has been impaired by mental disease.

Diagnostic Interpretation:

The presence of Anti-HAV, HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, and Anti-HCV antibodies can provide valuable information about the type and stage of hepatitis infection. question: Hardness of stone surface is affected by?
exp:
Colloidal systems such as agar and alginate retard the setting of gypsum products. If these materials are in contact with CaSO4·½H2O during setting, a soft, easily abraded surface is obtained. Accelerators such as potassium sulfate are added to improve the surface quality of the set CaSO4·2H2O against agar or alginate.
These colloids do not retard the setting by altering the solubility ratio of the hemihydrate and dihydrate forms, but rather by being adsorbed on the hemihydrate and dihydrate nucleation sites, thus interfering in the hydration reaction. The adsorption of these materials on the nucleating sites retards the setting reaction more effectively than adsorption on the calcium sulfate hemihydrate.

question: In pregnancy, the most common cause of transient- diabetes insipidus is:
exp:
Diabetes insipidus can be caused by:
Deficiency of antiduretic hormone               Resistance of ADH action
                    ↓                                                                       ↓
Central diabetes insipidus                           Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

A transient form of DI occurs during pregnancy due to:

– Excessive placental production of vasopressinase
– Decreased hepatic clearance due to abnormal liver function there in case of:

Preeclampsia
Fatty liver
Hepatitis.


Approximately 60% of women with previously known DI worsen, 20% improve and 20% do not change during pregnancy.
Worsening is attributed to excessive placental vasopressinase production.
Some females with DI who develop placental insufficiency show DI improvement, which is attributed to decreased vasopressinase production by the damaged placenta.

Symptoms:

Polyuria (4-15 liters/day)
Intense thirst particularly for ice cold fluids.

Diagnosis: is confirmed by water deprivation test.
Treatment: of choice intranasal L-deamino 8D arginine vasopressin (DDAVP) which is a synthetic analogue of ADH and is resistant to vasopressinase.
question_upd: What is the most common cause of transient diabetes insipidus in pregnancy?
exp_upd:
Diabetes insipidus is a condition characterized by the deficiency or resistance of antiduretic hormone (ADH). This hormone plays a crucial role in regulating the body's water balance, and its absence or impaired function can lead to excessive urine production and intense thirst.

There are two main types of diabetes insipidus: central diabetes insipidus, which is caused by a deficiency of ADH, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which is caused by the resistance of ADH action.

During pregnancy, a transient form of diabetes insipidus can occur due to the excessive production of vasopressinase by the placenta. This can worsen the condition in approximately 60% of women with previously known diabetes insipidus, while 20% may experience an improvement. The worsening of symptoms is attributed to the excessive production of vasopressinase, while the improvement is thought to be due to the decreased production of vasopressinase by the damaged placenta.

The symptoms of diabetes insipidus include polyuria, which is the production of large amounts of urine (typically 4-15 liters per day), and intense thirst, particularly for ice-cold fluids. The diagnosis of diabetes insipidus is confirmed by a water deprivation test, and the treatment of choice is intranasal L-deamino 8D arginine vasopressin (DDAVP), a synthetic analogue of ADH that is resistant to vasopressinase.

question: A man comes with aphasia. He is unable to name things and repetition is poor. However comprehension, fluency and understanding written words is unaffected. He is probably suffering from:
exp: Ans: D. Conduction aphasia(Ref Harrison 19/e p 1 76, 18/e p302)Typical case of conduction aphasia with normal comprehension & fluency, but impaired naming & repetition.Conduction aphasia:Due to damaged arcuate fasciculus.Arcuate fasciculus:Connection between Wernicke's (language comprehension) & Broca's (Language production) areas.Hence, connection lost.Clinical features:Hallmark finding - Inability to repeat words.Comprehension & language expression intact.Inability to transfer understood word to Broca 's area to be expressed.Results in meaningful fluent speech & relatively good comprehension but very poor repetition.
question_upd: Which type of aphasia is characterized by the inability to name objects or words, with poor repetition, but preserved comprehension, fluency, and ability to understand written words?
exp_upd:
Conduction aphasia is a type of aphasia characterized by normal comprehension and fluency, but impaired naming and repetition. This condition is caused by damage to the arcuate fasciculus, a connection between Wernicke's area (responsible for language comprehension) and Broca's area (responsible for language production).

The hallmark feature of conduction aphasia is the inability to repeat words. Despite having intact comprehension and language expression, individuals with conduction aphasia struggle to transfer understood words to Broca's area, resulting in meaningful, fluent speech and relatively good comprehension, but very poor repetition.

question:
The principal reason for placing an aluminium filter in
the primary beam of radiation is to:
exp:
Although an x-ray beam consists of a continuous spectrum of x-ray photon energies, only photons with sufficient energy to penetrate through anatomic structures and reach the image receptor (digital or film) are useful for diagnostic radiology. Low-energy photons that cannot reach the receptor contribute to patient risk but do no offer any benefit. Consequently, it is desirable to remove these low-energy photons from the beam. This removal can be accomplished in part by placing a metallic disk (filter) in the beam path. 
A filter preferentially removes low-energy photons from the beam, while allowing high energy photons that are able to contribute to making an image to pass through. 
Ref: Oral Radiology, Principles and Interpretation / Stuart C. White, Michael J. Pharoah - 7th ed - pg - 10

exp_upd:
Clinical manifestations of vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) typically appear in children between the ages of 2 and 3 years, with a higher incidence in females. In fact, VUR is often present from birth, but its detection is usually delayed until the child is 2-3 years old, with females typically showing symptoms earlier.

Patients with primary VUR often present with symptoms of pyelonephritis or cystitis, while those with secondary VUR may exhibit manifestations of underlying primary diseases. Notably, VUR is the most common cause of pyelonephritis, affecting 30-50% of patients with this condition. In addition, VUR is present in over 75% of individuals with radiological evidence of chronic pyelonephritis.

The most effective method for diagnosing VUR is the micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG), which not only detects the grade of reflux but also provides detailed information about urethral anatomy. Radionuclide imaging is another useful technique for detecting VUR, although it lacks the anatomic detail provided by MCUG. Due to its lower radiation exposure, radionuclide imaging is often used for follow-up purposes after an initial MCUG diagnosis.

question: Crude Bih rate for a sub-center is 20. What the number of pregnant woman registered in sub-center?
exp: Population of a sub-centre =5000 Crude bih rate= 20 per 1000 mid-year population Therefore, no. of bihs= 20/1000 x 5000=100 Pregnancy wastage factor = 10% (i.e. not all pregnancies result in a live bih, and roughly 10% ANC women have a "wastage" of their pregnancy. Therefore, total ANC= 100+ =110 As a thumb rule, Minimum number of ANC that should be registered at a time= 50%. - Min. No. registered in the sub-centre= 110 x 50/100=55 ~ ~60
question_upd: What is the number of pregnant women registered in a sub-center with a crude birth rate of 20?
exp_upd: The population of a sub-centre is 5,000. The crude birth rate is 20 births per 1,000 mid-year population. To calculate the number of births, multiply the crude birth rate by the population: 20/1,000 x 5,000 = 100. question: Root value of cremaster reflex is
exp: In Men, Cremaster muscle & cremaster fascia form middle/2nd covering of spermatic cord. This muscle & Its associated fascia are supplied by genital branch of GENITOFEMORAL NERVE(L1 L2) Contraction of this muscle & resulting elevation of testis can be stimulated by reflex arc Gently touching the skin at & around the anterior aspect of superior pa of thigh stimulates sensory fibers in femoral branch of genito-femoral N/ Ilio-Inguinal N. These fibers enter spinal cord at L1 At L1, Sensory fibers stimulate motor fibers carried in genital branch of genito-femoral N, which results in contraction of cremaster muscle & elevation of testis. Cremasteric reflex is more active in children, tending to diminish with age. As with many reflexes, it may be absent in ceain neurological disorders. Although, it can be used for testing spinal cord function at level L1 in men, Its clinical use is limited.
question_upd: What is the root value of the cremaster reflex?
exp_upd:
The cremaster muscle and its associated fascia form the middle layer of the spermatic cord in men. This muscle and fascia are supplied by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, which originates from the L1 and L2 vertebrae. When the cremaster muscle contracts, it elevates the testis, a process that can be stimulated by a reflex arc.

The sensory fibers responsible for this reflex are located in the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the ilio-inguinal nerve. These fibers enter the spinal cord at the L1 level, where they stimulate the motor fibers carried in the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve. This stimulation results in the contraction of the cremaster muscle and the elevation of the testis.

The cremasteric reflex is more active in children and tends to diminish with age. Like many reflexes, it may be absent in certain neurological disorders. Although it can be used to test spinal cord function at the L1 level in men, its clinical use is limited.

Autoimmune hepatitis is a condition characterized by a range of clinical features that can be similar to those seen in chronic viral hepatitis. Common symptoms include fatigue, malaise, anorexia, amenorrhea, acne, ahralgias, and jaundice. In some cases, patients may also experience ahritis, maculopapular eruptions (including cutaneous vasculitis), erythema nodosum, colitis, pleurisy, pericarditis, anemia, azotemia, and sicca syndrome.

There are three types of autoimmune hepatitis, each with distinct characteristics. Type I is associated with marked hyperglobulinemia, lupoid features, circulating antinuclear antibodies (ANAs), and HLA-DR3 or HLA-DR4 (especially HLA-DRB1*03). Associated autoantibodies include those against actin and atypical pANCA. Type II is linked to HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQBI haplotypes and is characterized by anti-LKM1. Type III, on the other hand, lacks ANA and anti-LKM1 but is marked by circulating antibodies to soluble liver antigen/liver pancreas antigen.

It is of a toxic child with a sho history of sorethroat, inspiratory stridor, muffled voice and droolingdue to odynophagia and dysphagia. Left untreated thereis progressive respiratory distress. The child is febrile. It is commonest between the ages of 2 and 8 Nebulized epinephrine (1mL of 1 in 1000 epinephrinediluted in 3mL of 0.9% saline) has an established role inthe acute paediatric airway in reducing mucosal oedemaby an alpha-agonist effect causing vasoconstriction andbronchodilation; a maximum effect is achieved within30-60 minutes. question_upd: What treatment, in addition to general airway management, is recommended for a child presenting with high-grade fever, inspiratory stridor, and swallowing difficulty with drooling of saliva, a condition that has developed over the past 4-6 hours?
exp_upd:
Acute epiglottitis is characterized by a distinctive presentation. It typically involves a toxic child with a short history of sore throat, inspiratory stridor, a muffled voice, and drooling due to odynophagia and dysphagia. If left untreated, the condition can progress to severe respiratory distress. The child is usually febrile, and the condition is most common between the ages of 2 and 8.

Nebulized epinephrine, diluted in 0.9% saline, has been established as a treatment option in the acute pediatric airway. This medication works by causing vasoconstriction and bronchodilation through its alpha-agonist effect, reducing mucosal edema. The maximum effect is achieved within 30-60 minutes, which may postpone or eliminate the need for an artificial airway or provide symptomatic relief until effective treatment can be administered.

question: NESTROFT test is a screening test for –
exp:
NESTROFT ( Naked Eye Single Tube Red Cell Osmotic Fragility Test) is a screening test for detection of beta thalassemia trait.

Thalassemia screening

Widespead prevlence of thalessemia has led to a pressing demand for community, screening.
Various methods for screening of thalassemia trait are available which include peripheral smear examination, RBC indices, 1VIeintzer's fraction, discriminant functions, NESTROFT etc.
NESTROFT TEST is used in many centres in India for screening of thalassemia trait.
If mother is NESTROFT positive, the confirmatory test for HbA2 is done for mother and the father is subjected to screening by NESTROFT. If father is also NESTROFT positive, confirmatory test for HbA2 is done for father.
If both the parents have thalessemia trait, there is 1:4 chance of fetus having thalassemia major.
Therefore, prenatal diagnosis is done by chorionic villus sampling (CVS) in first trimester.
If CVS confirms the fetus to be having thalasemia major, termination of pregnancy is indicated after counseling the parents.
If the fetus has thalassemia minor (trait) pregnancy is continued as such and baby will have normal lifespan.
It is worth noting here that a positive NESTROFT test is seen in other conditions beside beta thalassemia trait. These are iron deficiency anemia, alpha thalassemia trait, homozygous and heterozygous HbE, HbS as well as hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin.

Therefore, a positive NESTROFT test should always be followed by a confirmatory test for HBA2 ( eg. serum electrophoresis).

exp_upd:
Here is the rewritten text:

The widespread prevalence of thalassemia has led to a pressing demand for community screening. Various methods are available for screening thalassemia trait, including peripheral smear examination, RBC indices, and NESTROFT. NESTROFT is a widely used screening test in many centers in India for detecting beta thalassemia trait.

If a mother tests positive for NESTROFT, a confirmatory test for HbA2 is performed for the mother, and the father is screened using NESTROFT. If the father is also positive, a confirmatory test for HbA2 is performed for the father. If both parents have thalassemia trait, there is a 1:4 chance of the fetus having thalassemia major.

Prenatal diagnosis is performed by chorionic villus sampling (CVS) in the first trimester. If CVS confirms the fetus has thalassemia major, termination of pregnancy is indicated after counseling the parents. If the fetus has thalassemia minor (trait), the pregnancy can be continued, and the baby will have a normal lifespan.

It is essential to note that a positive NESTROFT test can also be seen in conditions other than beta thalassemia trait, such as iron deficiency anemia, alpha thalassemia trait, and hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin. Therefore, a positive NESTROFT test should always be followed by a confirmatory test for HbA2, such as serum electrophoresis.

question: Which amino acid does not include post translational modification?
exp: Selenocysteine (21st amino acid) & Pyrrolysine (22nd amino acid) Formed by co-translational modification Not by post-translational modifications. Selenocysteine and Pyrrolysine 21st amino acid-Selenocysteine- UGA 22nd amino acid - Pyrrolysine - UAG Both UGA, UAG are stop codon but co-translational modification can give rise to amino acid selenocysteine and pyrrolysine. co-translational modification. Enzymes that use selenocysteine as their active sites are called Seleno Proteins. Selenocysteine containing proteins: Glutathione peroxidase Thioredoxin reductase selenoprotein P 5' deiodinases
question_upd: Which amino acid does not undergo post-translational modification?
exp_upd:
Selenocysteine, the 21st amino acid, and pyrrolysine, the 22nd amino acid, are formed through a process called co-translational modification, which occurs during protein synthesis and is distinct from post-translational modifications. Both selenocysteine and pyrrolysine are encoded by the codons UGA and UAG, respectively, which are typically recognized as stop codons. However, co-translational modification can override this default termination signal, allowing these amino acids to be incorporated into proteins.

Enzymes that utilize selenocysteine as their active site are referred to as selenoproteins. Examples of selenocysteine-containing proteins include glutathione peroxidase, thioredoxin reductase, selenoprotein P, and 5' deiodinases.

question_upd: Which of the following is not a reason why the injured nerve is unable to regenerate in a patient who has suffered a spinal cord injury at the level of T8, resulting in loss of sensation below the level of the lesion?
exp_upd: Following CNS injuries, several events create an environment that inhibits regeneration. Astrocytic proliferation, activation of microglia, scar formation, inflammation, and invasion of immune cells all contribute to an unfavorable environment for regeneration. Additionally, CNS neurons lack the growth-promoting chemical needed to facilitate regeneration, and CNS myelin is a potent inhibitor of axonal growth. As a result, the proximal stump of a damaged axon in the CNS will form short sprouts, but distant stump recovery is rare, and the damaged axons are unlikely to form new synapses. This is why treatment of brain and spinal cord injuries often focuses on rehabilitation rather than reversing the nerve damage.

question: A condition where there is loss of interdental bone on facial and lingual plate, without involvement of radicular bone is:
exp:
Reversed Architecture
Reverse (or negative) alveolar bone architecture is the result of a loss  of  interdental  bone,  without  a  concomitant  loss  of  radicular (buccal or lingual/palatal) bone, thereby reversing the normal (or positive)  architecture .  Negative  architecture  is  more common in the maxilla of patients with periodontitis.
Ledges
Ledges are plateau-like bone margins that are caused by the resorption of thickened bony plates .
Osseous Craters
Osseous craters are a specific type of two-wall defect; they present as concavities in the crest of the interdental bone that is confined within the facial and lingual walls. Craters have been found to make up about one-third (35.2%) of all defects and about two-thirds (62%) of all mandibular defects; they occur twice as often in posterior segments as in anterior segments.
Ref: Newman and Carranza’s Clinical Periodontology, thirteenth edition; page no 325

exp: Question mentions - H/o smoker first thing that comes in mind is COPD & MC arrhythmia atrial fibrillation. We first see lead II on ECG RR approx. 1.5 and more towards left 2.5. D/D Atrial fibrillation Multifocal atrial tachycardia P wave absent P wave present Variable RR interval Therefore ruled out P wave varying amplitual and answer is MAT. Trick to solve: First check if patient has tachycardia/bradycardia RR interval Narrow QRS suggests supraventricular tachycardia COPD is the reason for multifocal atrial tachycardia due to right ventricular strain causing RV enlargement causing right axis duration. Visible P wave variable amplitude RR interval changing Narrow QRS All point towards diagnosis of multifocal atrial tachycardia. Monomorphic VT is ruled out as it has broad QRS complex. Between MAT & AV nodal reentrant tachycardia the H/o smokers narrows down the diagnosis to MAT.
question_upd: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 50-year-old tall, thin smoker who presents with dyspnea and palpitations, as revealed by an electrocardiogram (ECG)?
exp_upd:
Here is the rewritten text:

When a patient with a history of smoking is evaluated, atrial fibrillation and multifocal atrial tachycardia are often the first conditions that come to mind. The electrocardiogram (ECG) shows a lead II tracing with a heart rate (HR) of 300 beats per minute (bpm) and a regular rhythm (RR) interval of approximately 1.5 seconds, which is more pronounced on the left side at 2.5 seconds. This indicates tachycardia with a variable RR interval. The differential diagnosis includes atrial fibrillation, multifocal atrial tachycardia, and P wave absence or presence. The presence of a variable RR interval and the absence of a P wave suggest multifocal atrial tachycardia. The patient's history of smoking, which can cause right ventricular strain and enlargement, leading to a right axis deviation, is a key factor in this diagnosis. The ECG findings, including a narrow QRS complex, variable amplitude P wave, and changing RR interval, all support the diagnosis of multifocal atrial tachycardia. Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is ruled out due to its characteristic broad QRS complex. The patient's history of smoking narrows the differential diagnosis to multifocal atrial tachycardia, making it the most likely diagnosis.

question: Target sign is seen in?
exp: Leakage of CSF into the nose is called CSF rhinorrhea. It may be clear fluid or mixed with blood as in acute head injuries. TRAUMA. Most of the cases follow trauma.it can be accidental or surgical. Inflammation, mucoceles of sinuses, sinunasal polyposis, fungal infection of sinuses & osteomyelitis, can all erode the bone and dura. Neoplasms, idiopathic- where cause is unknown and patient has spontaneous leak. SITE OF Leakage- CSF from anterior cranial fossa reaches the nose (1) cribriform plate, (2) roof of ethmoid air cells or (3) frontal sinus. CSF from middle cranial fossa follows injuries to sphenoid sinus, cribriform plate. In fracture of temporal bone, CSF reaches the middle ear and then escapes through the Eustachian tube into the nose (CSF OTORHINORRHOEA) DIAGNOSIS- there is history of clear watery discharge from the nose on bending the head or straining. CSF rhinorrhea should be differentiated from nasal discharge as the former is sudden, gushes in drops when bending and cannot be sniffed back. CSF rhinorrhea after head trauma is mixed with blood and shows "target sign" when collected on filter paper.it shows central red spot and peripheral lighter halo sign. LAB TEST = BETA-2 transferrin is seen in CSF and not in the nasal discharge. its presence is a specific and sensitive test.
question_upd: What is the condition in which the Target sign is typically seen?
exp_upd:
Leakage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) into the nose is called CSF rhinorrhea. This condition may manifest as clear fluid or mixed with blood, typically occurring in the aftermath of acute head injuries. Most cases of CSF rhinorrhea are associated with trauma, which can be accidental or surgical in nature.

The erosion of bone and dura can be caused by various factors, including inflammation, mucoceles of sinuses, sinunasal polyposis, fungal infections of sinuses, and osteomyelitis. Neoplasms and idiopathic cases, where the cause is unknown, can also lead to spontaneous CSF leaks.

The site of leakage is typically located in the anterior cranial fossa, where CSF from this region can reach the nose through the cribriform plate, roof of ethmoid air cells, or frontal sinus. Injuries to the sphenoid sinus and cribriform plate can also lead to CSF leakage from the middle cranial fossa. In rare cases, a fracture of the temporal bone can cause CSF to reach the middle ear and then escape through the Eustachian tube into the nose, a condition known as CSF otorhinorrhea.

Diagnosis of CSF rhinorrhea is often made based on a patient's history of clear, watery discharge from the nose, which is exacerbated by bending or straining. This condition should be differentiated from nasal discharge, as CSF rhinorrhea is characterized by sudden, gush-like episodes that cannot be sniffed back. In cases of CSF rhinorrhea following head trauma, the discharge is often mixed with blood and may exhibit a "target sign" when collected on filter paper, featuring a central red spot surrounded by a lighter halo.

A specific and sensitive laboratory test for CSF rhinorrhea is the presence of beta-2 transferrin in the CSF, which is not found in nasal discharge.

question: Bullet fingerprinting is:
exp: Bullet fingerprinting- Primary markings- The rifled firearm leaves its signature on the caridge case and on the bullet. With all rifled firearms, the bullet is slightly larger than the barrel, and as it passes through the barrel, its sides are marked by the rifling of the barrel. Secondary markings- They are produced on the surface of the bullet by imperfection on the inner surface of the barrel. These irregularities are produced by sticking of paicles of the bullet to the bore when shots are fired and is known as metallic fouling. They also result accidentally during the manufacturing process, usually microscopic in nature and have random distribution. They are useful in identifying the specific gun which was fired.
question_upd: What is the primary marking on a bullet?
exp_upd:
Bullet Fingerprinting

The rifled firearm leaves its signature on the cartridge case and on the bullet. This signature is composed of two types of markings: primary and secondary.

Primary Markings
The rifling of the barrel marks the sides of the bullet as it passes through the barrel. Due to the rifled firearm's design, the bullet is slightly larger than the barrel.

Secondary Markings
These markings are produced on the surface of the bullet by imperfections on the inner surface of the barrel. These imperfections can be caused by the sticking of particles of the bullet to the bore when shots are fired, known as metallic fouling. They can also result from accidental occurrences during the manufacturing process, typically microscopic in nature and having a random distribution. These secondary markings are useful in identifying the specific gun that was fired.

exp: The answer is A Acute pyelonephritis is a bacterial infection causing inflammation of the kidneys and is one of the most common diseases of the kidney.Pyelonephritis occurs as a complication of an ascending urinary tract infection (UTI) which spreads from the bladder to the kidneys and their collecting systems.Symptoms usually include fever, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, burning on urination, increased frequency, and urgency. The 2 most common symptoms are usually fever and flank pain. E. coli is the most common bacteria causing acute pyelonephritis due to its unique ability to adhere to and colonize the urinary tract and kidneys.Histopathology will usually reveal necrosis or putrid abscess formation within the renal parenchyma. The renal tissues are infiltrated with neutrophils, macrophages and plasma cells. However, architecture is not completely disorganized.The presence of white blood cells within or upon casts strongly suggests pyelonephritis, direct infection of the kidney. exp_upd:
Acute pyelonephritis is a bacterial infection that causes inflammation of the kidneys, making it one of the most common diseases affecting the kidney. This condition typically develops as a complication of an ascending urinary tract infection (UTI), which spreads from the bladder to the kidneys and their collecting systems. Symptoms of acute pyelonephritis usually include fever, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, burning on urination, increased frequency, and urgency. Fever and flank pain are the most common symptoms. E. coli is the most common bacteria responsible for acute pyelonephritis, due to its ability to adhere to and colonize the urinary tract and kidneys.

Histopathological examination typically reveals necrosis or putrid abscess formation within the renal parenchyma. The renal tissues are infiltrated with neutrophils, macrophages, and plasma cells, although the architecture is not completely disorganized. The presence of white blood cells within or upon casts is a strong indication of pyelonephritis, which is a direct infection of the kidney. However, white blood cells may also be present in other inflammatory conditions, such as acute allergic interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, or post-streptococcal acute glomerulonephritis.

question: All are true about rheumatic fever, except –
exp:
Rheumatic fever

Rheumatic fever is an acute immunologically mediated multisystem inflammatory disease that occurs few weeks after an episode of group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
The disease is immune mediated, not a communicable disease.
	Epidemiology ofAcute Rheumatic fever.
The epidemiology of acute Rheumatic fever is identical to that of group A streptococcal upper respiratory tract infection.
As is the case of streptococcal sore throat, acute rheumatic fever most often occurs in children, the peak age related incidence is between 5-15 years.
Epidemiological risk factor for rheumatic fever, include lower standards of living especially crowding, the disease has been more common among socially and economically disadvantaged populations.

Pathogenesis of Rheumatic fever

It is strongly suspected that acute Rheumatic fever is a hypersensitivity reaction induced by group A streptococci but the exact pathogenesis remains uncertain despite many years of investigation.
Although the precise factor or factors that confer this property are unknown, highly rheumatogenic strains, share certain biological characteristic.
It is believed that antibodies directed against the M proteins of certain strains cross reacts with glycoprotein antigens in the heart, joints and other tissues. These strains are (1, 3, 5, 6, 18).
The M proteins molecules has a particular surface exposed antigenic domain against which Rheumatic fever patients mount a strong antibody response. These antibodies against the M proteins cross reacts with glycoproteins antigens in the heart, joints and other tissues because these glycoproteins share similar features with M antigenic domain.
question_upd: Which of the following is not true about rheumatic fever?
exp_upd:
Rheumatic fever is an acute, immunologically mediated, multisystem inflammatory disease that occurs several weeks after an episode of group A streptococcal pharyngitis. This disease is immune-mediated, not a communicable disease.

The epidemiology of acute rheumatic fever is identical to that of group A streptococcal upper respiratory tract infection. The disease most often occurs in children, with the peak age-related incidence between 5-15 years. Risk factors for rheumatic fever include lower standards of living, particularly crowding, and the disease has been more common among socially and economically disadvantaged populations.

The pathogenesis of rheumatic fever is believed to be a hypersensitivity reaction induced by group A streptococci. Although the exact mechanism is uncertain, highly rheumatogenic strains share certain biological characteristics. It is thought that antibodies directed against the M proteins of these strains cross-react with glycoprotein antigens in the heart, joints, and other tissues. These strains include types 1, 3, 5, 6, and 18. The M protein molecules have a particular surface-exposed antigenic domain against which rheumatic fever patients mount a strong antibody response. These antibodies against the M proteins cross-react with glycoprotein antigens in the heart, joints, and other tissues because these glycoproteins share similar features with the M antigenic domain.

question: The case of biliary duct stricture with retching and vomiting, given 3mg morphine epiduraly daily, one day 12 mg mistakenly dose of epidural, morphine given. Not present:-
exp: Side effect of high dose epidural opioid: Nausea and vomiting Pruritis Urinary retention Respiratory depression High dose of opioid can spread centrally and stimulate CTZ center and can precipitate nausea and vomiting. Pruritis due to morphine is not due to histamine release, high dose morphine can spread centrally, act on trigeminal nerve and cause pruritis. Urinary retention in morphine use is due to it's action on sacral spinal cord, therefore it can happen even at normal dose and not related to high dose. Respiratory depression in morphine overdose due to migration of morphine centrally.
question_upd: Which of the following symptoms is NOT present in a patient with a biliary duct stricture who experiences retching and vomiting, and who has been mistakenly given a 12mg dose of epidural morphine, having previously received 3mg daily, except for:
exp_upd:
High-dose epidural opioid administration can lead to several side effects, including nausea and vomiting, pruritis, urinary retention, and respiratory depression.

Nausea and vomiting are caused by the central spread of the opioid, which stimulates the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) in the brain. Pruritis, or itching, is a result of the opioid's action on the trigeminal nerve, rather than histamine release. Urinary retention, on the other hand, is a direct effect of the opioid on the sacral spinal cord, and can occur even at normal doses. Finally, respiratory depression in morphine overdose is a result of the opioid's central migration, which can lead to a decrease in respiratory rate and depth.

question_upd: Which of the following is true about antigenic drift?
exp_upd:
Antigenic drift is a mechanism for variation in viruses that involves the accumulation of mutations within genes that code for antibody binding sites. This process results from genetic recombination of human with animal or another virus, leading to a major antigenic change. This can cause a major epidemic or pandemic involving most or all age groups.

Antigenic drift occurs through point mutations in the genes, driven by selection pressure from immunity in the host population. This results in a new strain of virus particles that cannot be inhibited as effectively by the antibodies originally targeted against previous strains. This makes it easier for the virus to spread throughout a partially immune population, responsible for seasonal epidemics of influenza.

Osteoclasts are characterized by a plasma membrane showing multiple folds, also known as ruffled borders. This unique structure is involved in osteocytic resorption. Osteoclasts are large, polymorphic cells with 20 or more oval, closely packed nuclei. Howship's lacunae, which lie in close contact with the bone surface in resorption bays, are also a distinctive feature of osteoclasts. The cytoplasm of osteoclasts contains numerous coated transport vesicles and microtubule arrays, which are involved in the transport of vesicles between Golgi stacks and the ruffled membrane.

In contrast, osteoblasts are derived from osteoprogenitor (stem) cells of mesenchymal origin and are present in bone marrow and other connective tissues. They proliferate and differentiate after being stimulated by bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), which induce their transformation into osteoblasts prior to bone formation.

exp_upd:
The World Health Organization (WHO) classification system categorizes periapical lesions into several categories. Acute Apical Periodontitis (Ko 4.4) is a condition characterized by inflammation and infection of the apical region of a tooth, typically resulting from bacterial invasion of the pulp. Chronic Apical Periodontitis (Ko 4.5) is a more persistent and often asymptomatic condition, where the apical region of a tooth becomes chronically inflamed and infected.

Periapical Abscesses (Ko 4.6) can develop with or without sinus formation. When a sinus forms, it can drain into various locations, including the maxillary antrum (Ko 4.60), nasal floor (Ko 4.61), oral cavity (Ko 4.62), or outer skin of the face (Ko 4.63). Periapical Abscesses without sinus formation (Ko 4.7) can also occur. Additionally, Periapical Cysts (Ko 4.8) can develop, which are non-inflamed, fluid-filled sacs that can be apical or lateral (Ko 4.80), residual (Ko 4.81), or inflammatory paradental (Ko 4.82).

question: Which TCA intermediate is used in haem synthesis:
exp: Solutions: - The first step of haem synthesis uses succinyl CoA which is intermediate to TCA. Fumarate, Alpha keto gluterate and malate (4C) is also intermediate to TCA. Malonate (3C) or malonyl CoA is inhibitor of 3 pathways in body - Succinate DH of TCA - Complex 2 of ETC - Beta oxidation of Fatty acid Acetyl CoA is not an intermediate of TCA. Haem synthesis It occurs in Mitochondria + cytoplasm (So, doesn't occurs in RBC)
question_upd: Which TCA intermediate is used in haem synthesis?
exp_upd:
Haem synthesis is a complex process that involves the conversion of succinyl CoA, an intermediate of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, into haem. The TCA cycle is a critical pathway in cellular metabolism, and its intermediates, including fumarate, alpha-ketoglutarate, and malate, play important roles in various cellular processes.

Malonate, a 3-carbon compound, serves as an inhibitor of three distinct pathways in the body: succinate dehydrogenase of the TCA cycle, complex II of the electron transport chain, and beta oxidation of fatty acids. In contrast, acetyl CoA, a key intermediate in fatty acid metabolism, is not an intermediate of the TCA cycle.

Haem synthesis occurs in both the mitochondria and cytoplasm, but it does not occur in red blood cells (RBCs).

The hypothalamus contains two types of magnocellular (large) neurons that synthesize ADH in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus, about five sixths in the supraoptic nuclei and about one sixth in the paraventricular nuclei. The most important renal action of ADH is to increase the water permeability  of  the  distal  tubule,  collecting  tubule, and collecting duct epithelia. This effect helps the body to conserve water in circumstances such as dehydration. In the absence of ADH, the permeability of the distal tubules and collecting ducts to water is low, causing the kidneys to excrete large amounts of dilute urine, a condition called diabetes insipidus. Thus, the actions of ADH play a key role in controlling the degree of dilution or concentration of the urine.

exp: Ans: B. Onchocerca volvulus Adult stage of Onchocerca volvulus filarial worms does not cause any illness or disease.Onchocerciasis:Primarily affects skin, eyes & lymph nodes.In contrast to pathology in lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis damage elicited by microfilariae & not by adult parasites.Onchocerca microfilariae:Released from female worms causing most severe damage.Migrating microfilariae (exclusively found in interstitial fluids of skin & subdermal tissues not bloodstream).Cause changes in skin pigment & loss of elastic fibers a "hanging groin, severe intractable & intolerable pruritus.Blindness (primarily men) develops over many years - Due to microfilariae accumulation in vitreous humor.Are not blood borne & hence, concentrate & remain in eye.Visual clouding, photophobia & ultimately retinal damage a Incurable blindness.(Ref: Harrison 19/e p1420).
question_upd: Which of the following filarial worms is **not** responsible for diseases in the adult stage?
exp_upd: The adult stage of Onchocerca volvulus filarial worms does not cause any illness or disease. Onchocerciasis primarily affects the skin, eyes, and lymph nodes. In contrast to the pathology in lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis damage is elicited by microfilariae, not by adult parasites. Onchocerca microfilariae are released from female worms and cause the most severe damage. Migrating microfilariae are exclusively found in the interstitial fluids of the skin and subdermal tissues, not in the bloodstream. They cause changes in skin pigment and loss of elastic fibers, leading to conditions such as "hanging groin" and severe, intractable, and intolerable pruritus. Blindness, primarily affecting men, develops over many years due to the accumulation of microfilariae in the vitreous humor. The microfilariae are not blood-borne and concentrate and remain in the eye, causing visual clouding, photophobia, and ultimately, retinal damage, which is incurable.

question: Central value of a set of 180 values can be obtained by
exp:
Quartile: Divides a distribution into 4 equal parts, so the number of intercepts required will be 3, i.e. Q1, Q2, Q3

– So, Zero – Q1 covers 25% values
– Similarly, Q2 – Q1, Q3 – Q2 and 100 – Q3 all cover 25% values each
– Thus, Q2 – Zero, 100 – Q2 and Q3 – Q1 all cover 50% values each
– Q1 divides a distribution in a ratio of 25 : 75 OR 1 : 3
– Q2 divides a distribution in a ratio of 50 : 50 OR 1 : 1, Thus second quartile is equivalent to median
– Q3 divides a distribution in a ratio of 75 : 25 OR 3 : 1.
In the given question, n = 180
Thus Q2 which is equivalent to median, divides a distribution in a ratio of 50 : 50 OR 1 : 1.
question_upd: What is the central value that can be obtained by analyzing a set of 180 values?
exp_upd:
A quartile is a statistical measure that divides a distribution into four equal parts. This means that the number of intercepts required will be three, including Q1, Q2, and Q3.

Q1, Q2, and Q3 each cover 25% of the values in the distribution. Additionally, Q2, which is equivalent to the median, divides the distribution in a ratio of 50% to 50%, or 1:1. Q1 divides the distribution in a ratio of 25% to 75%, or 1:3, while Q3 divides it in a ratio of 75% to 25%, or 3:1.

The infant mortality rate for the sub-centre is calculated by multiplying the number of live births by the infant mortality rate, divided by 1,000. For calculation purposes, assume an infant mortality rate of 34 per 1,000. This results in 3.5 infant deaths, or approximately 4 infant deaths.

Therefore, the total number of infants is 102 minus 4, which equals 98.

question: All are signs of impending Eisenmenger except –
exp:
Eisenmenger syndrome refers to patients with a VSD in which blood is shunted from right to left as a result of development of pulmonary vascular resistance. Initially shunt is from left to right as the systemic vascular pressure is greater than pulmonary vascular pressure. With time pulmonary vascular resistance increases due to change in pulmonary vessel wall as a result of increased flow in pulmonary vessels. When pulmonary vascular pressure exceeds the systemic vascular resistance, reversal of shunt into right to left shunt occurs.
This development of right to left shunt due to reversal of left to right shunt as a result of development of pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary hypertension is called Eisenmenger syndrome.

exp_upd: Eisenmenger syndrome is a condition that occurs in patients with a ventricular septal defect (VSD), where blood is shunted from the right to the left side of the heart due to the development of pulmonary vascular resistance. Initially, the shunt is from the left to the right side, as the systemic vascular pressure is greater than the pulmonary vascular pressure. Over time, the pulmonary vascular resistance increases due to changes in the pulmonary vessel wall, which result from the increased flow in the pulmonary vessels. When the pulmonary vascular pressure exceeds the systemic vascular pressure, the shunt reverses, and blood begins to flow from the right to the left side of the heart. This development of a right to left shunt, resulting from the reversal of the initial left to right shunt due to the development of pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary hypertension, is known as Eisenmenger syndrome.

exp_upd:
Here is the rewritten text:

The term "false virgin" refers to a situation where a woman's hymen is intact, but it is thick and has been broken due to sexual intercourse. In this case, the labia majora are flabby and may gap when the thighs are abducted. The labia minora are loose and have a blackish-brown color. The vagina is deep, roomy, and dilated, with a less rugose wall that can easily accommodate two fingers.

In contrast, a true virgin has labia majora that are firm, rounded, and complete. The labia minora are soft, sensitive, and pink in color. The fourchette and posterior commissure are intact, and the vaginal wall is closely approximated. The vaginal mucosa is rugose, reddish, and sensitive to touch. The hymen is also intact.

During this period, the fetus's nails are thick, and its eyelids are open, with the pupillary membrane having disappeared. The skin is dusky-red, thick, and fibrous. Meconium, a substance produced by the fetus, is present in the entire large intestine.

Additionally, the testes are located at the external inguinal ring, and the gallbladder contains bile. The caecum, a part of the large intestine, is visible in the right iliac fossa. Finally, ossification centers are present in the talus, a bone in the ankle.

question_upd: Which of the following cardiac defects is characterized by ductus-independent blood flow?
exp_upd:
Congenital heart disease in newborns can be broadly categorized based on the relationship between the patient's cardiac defect and the patent ductus arteriosus, resulting in four distinct groups.

**Pulmonary Flow Ductal Dependence**

Newborns with congenital heart disease who rely on the potency of their ductus arteriosus for pulmonary blood flow exhibit varying degrees of cyanosis. This group includes conditions such as Critical Pulmonary Valve Stenosis with Intact Ventricular Septum, Li Tricuspid Atresia, and Tetralogy of Fallot.

**Systemic Flow Ductal Dependence**

Newborns who are dependent on their ductus arteriosus for systemic blood flow present with severely decreased cardiac output. This decreased systemic flow is characterized by pallor, diminished peripheral pulses, low urine output, cool extremities, and varying degrees of metabolic acidosis. This group includes conditions such as Congenital Valvular Aortic Stenosis, Coarctation of the Aorta, Interrupted Aortic Arch, and Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome (HLHS).

**Oxygenation Ductal Dependence**

These newborns are born with congenital heart disease that requires a patent ductus for adequate mixing of saturated and desaturated blood. This group includes conditions such as Transposition of the Great Vessels (TGV).

**Ductal Independence**

These neonates are not dependent on a patent ductus but still require urgent operation. This group includes conditions such as Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return (TAPVR), Truncus Arteriosus, and Anomalous Origin of the Left Main Coronary Artery from the Pulmonary Artery.
opa_upd: Transposition of great arteries with intact septum

However, if both AFP and AChE levels are elevated, it is indicative of an open NTD.

exp: Answer- B- Cover Uncover TestSince the diagnosis is latent strabismus the correct answer is B > Cover-uncover test. It tells about the presence and type of heterophoria. To perform it, one eye is covered with an occluder and the other is made to fix an object. In the presence of heterophoria, the eye under cover will dete. After a few seconds the cover is quickly removed and the movement of the eye (which was under cover) is observed. Direction of movement of the eyeball tells the type of heterophoria >The forced duction test is performed in order to determine whether the absence of movement of the eye is due to a neurological disorder or a mechanical restriction. question_upd: What test should be performed to assess the inward detion of both eyes in an 18-month-old child, who exhibits inward detion of both eyes on examination?
exp_upd:
The Cover-Uncover Test is a valuable diagnostic tool used to detect the presence and type of heterophoria. To perform this test, one eye is covered with an occluder, and the other eye is made to fixate on an object. In the presence of heterophoria, the eye under cover will deviate. After a few seconds, the cover is quickly removed, and the movement of the eye (which was under cover) is observed. The direction of movement of the eyeball indicates the type of heterophoria.

In addition to the Cover-Uncover Test, the Forced Duction Test is performed to determine whether the absence of eye movement is due to a neurological disorder or a mechanical restriction. This test involves grasping the anesthetized conjunctiva with forceps and attempting to move the eyeball in the direction where movement is restricted.

Fundus examination is also essential for diagnosing diseases of the vitreous, optic nerve head, retina, and choroid.

question: A neonate has central cyanosis and short systolic murmur on the 2nd day of birth. The diagnosis is –
exp:
Out of the four options, only 1st two are cyanotic heart disease i.e. TOF & TGV.
TOF can be ruled out as it does not cause cyanosis at birth.

Nelson says - "Often cyanosis is not present of birth, but with increasing hypertrophy of the right ventricular
infiindibulum and patient growth, Cyanosis occurs later in the 1st year of life."

Short systolic murmur is not of much help in reaching the diagnosis as it is present in both the conditions. Transposition of great vessels 
Transposition of great vessels is defined as : -

i) Aorta arising from right ventricle.
ii)Pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle.

Anatomically TGA is divided into :-

A) Complete variety

Right atrium is connected to right ventricle and right ventricle is connected to aorta.
Left atrium is connected to left ventricle and left ventricle is connected to pulmonary artery.
This results in complete separation of systemic and pulmonary circulation : -
question_upd: What is the most likely diagnosis for a neonate who presents with central cyanosis and a short systolic murmur on the second day of birth?
exp_upd:
Cyanotic heart disease can be classified into two main categories: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) and Tricuspid Atresia with Pulmonary Stenosis (TGV). TOF is distinguished from TGV because it does not typically cause cyanosis at birth. Instead, cyanosis often develops later in the first year of life, as the right ventricular infundibulum hypertrophies and the patient grows, as described by Nelson.

A short systolic murmur is not a reliable indicator for diagnosing these conditions, as it is present in both TOF and TGV. Transposition of the Great Vessels (TGA) is a distinct anatomical variation, characterized by:

i) The aorta arising from the right ventricle.
ii) The pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle.

Anatomically, TGA can be divided into two subcategories:

A) Complete variety

In this type, the right atrium is connected to the right ventricle, and the right ventricle is connected to the aorta. Meanwhile, the left atrium is connected to the left ventricle, and the left ventricle is connected to the pulmonary artery. This results in a complete separation of the systemic and pulmonary circulations.

question_upd: What are histopathological rosettes typically seen in?
exp_upd:
Rosettes are small, round groupings of cells found in tumors. They typically consist of cells arranged in a spoke-wheel or halo pattern surrounding a central, acellular region, which is commonly seen in retinoblastomas. In well-differentiated retinoblastomas, the tumor cells are characteristically arranged in rosettes. There are two types of rosettes: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, characterized by small tumor cells arranged around a lumen with their nuclei away from the lumen, and Homer-Wright rosettes, featuring a radial arrangement of tumor cells around a central neurofibrillar structure.

In contrast, PNETs (Primitive Neuro-Ectodermal Tumors) are composed of sheets of uniform, small, round cells that are slightly larger than lymphocytes. Medulloblastomas, on the other hand, are characterized by individual tumor cells that are small, with little cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei that are frequently elongated or crescent-shaped.

Acute intermittent porphyriaPeriodic abdominal pain (GI symptoms), peripheral neuropathy, headache (neurological symptoms) and psychiatric disorders (aggressive behavior) is highly suggestive of acute intermittent porphyria.Asymptomatic in majority of patients prior to pubeyMC symptom: Abdominal painIleus, abdominal distention & decreased bowel sounds are common.Nausea; vomiting; constipation; tachycardia; hypeension; mental symptoms; pain in limbs, head, neck, or chest; muscle weakness; sensory loss; dysuria; and urinary retention are characteristic.Tachycardia, hypeension, restlessness, tremors & excess sweating are due to sympathetic overactivity.Peripheral neuropathy is due to axonal degeneration and primarily affects motor neurons.Motor neuropathy affects the proximal muscles initially, more often in the shoulders & arms.Mental symptoms: Anxiety, insomnia, depression, disorientation, hallucinations, paranoia & seizures
question_upd: What is the most probable diagnosis for a 20-year-old female who presents with headaches, vomiting, and decreased movement in her right leg, with a history of episodes of violent and aggressive behavior and abdominal pain?
exp_upd:
Acute intermittent porphyria is a medical condition characterized by periodic episodes of abdominal pain, peripheral neuropathy, and psychiatric disorders. The symptoms can include abdominal pain, ileus, abdominal distension, and decreased bowel sounds, as well as nausea, vomiting, constipation, tachycardia, hypertension, mental symptoms, pain in the limbs, head, neck, or chest, muscle weakness, sensory loss, dysuria, and urinary retention.

The condition can also cause sympathetic overactivity, leading to symptoms such as tachycardia, hypertension, restlessness, tremors, and excessive sweating. Peripheral neuropathy, which is primarily caused by axonal degeneration and affects motor neurons, can cause motor neuropathy that initially affects the proximal muscles, particularly in the shoulders and arms.

Mental symptoms of acute intermittent porphyria can include anxiety, insomnia, depression, disorientation, hallucinations, paranoia, and seizures.

question: Absolute refractoriness of a neuron is due to?
exp: Absolute refractory period: The period during which 2nd action potential cannot be elicited, even with strong stimulus is called "ABSOLUTE REFRACTORY PERIOD". Reason for this restriction is that sholy after action potential is initiated, the sodium channels (or calcium channels / both) become inactivated & no amount of excitatory signal applied to these channels at this point will open inactivated gates. Only condition that will allow them to reopen is when membrane potential returns to or gets close to original resting membrane potential level. Then, within another small fraction of second, inactivated gates of channels open & new action potential can be initiated This period for large myelinated nerve fibers is about 1/2500 second thus, such fibers can transmit maximum of about 2500 impulses per second - Na have 2 gates, activated gate & an inactivated gate. At resting state - active gate - closed - inactive gate - open At stimulus - both gates are open At absolute refractory period - active gate - open; inactive gate - closed Next action potential is generated only after inactivated gate is open & both gates go back to resting state.
question_upd: What is the primary mechanism responsible for absolute refractoriness of a neuron?
exp_upd:
The absolute refractory period is the time during which a second action potential cannot be elicited, even with a strong stimulus. This restriction occurs because shortly after an action potential is initiated, sodium channels (or calcium channels, or both) become inactivated, and no amount of excitatory signal applied to these channels at this point will open the inactivated gates. The only condition that allows them to reopen is when the membrane potential returns to or approaches the original resting membrane potential level. Then, within a small fraction of a second, the inactivated gates of the channels open, and a new action potential can be initiated.

For large myelinated nerve fibers, this period is approximately 1/2500 of a second, allowing these fibers to transmit a maximum of about 2500 impulses per second. Sodium channels have two gates: an activated gate and an inactivated gate. At the resting state, the active gate is closed, and the inactive gate is open. When a stimulus is applied, both gates are open. During the absolute refractory period, the active gate is open, and the inactive gate is closed. The next action potential is generated only after the inactive gate is open, and both gates return to their resting state.

question: Percentage of surgical site infection in patients with clean contaminated wound after prophylactic antibiotic?
exp: Wounds classification: Clean - 5% Clean contaminated - 10% Contaminated - 20-30% Diy - 30-40% Wounds Class Definition I: Clean Uninfected operative wound without inflammation Respiratory, alimentary, genital or infected urinary tract is not entered Wounds are closed primarily, if necessary drained with closed drain Examples of Clean Wound Inguinal hernia Joint replacement Thyroidectomy Mastectomy Abdominal aoic aneurysm (AAA) repair II: Clean contaminated Operative wound in which respiratory tract GIT or genitourinary tract is entered under controlled condition without unusual contamination Examples of Clean Contaminated Wound Cholecystectomy CBD exploration Elective GI surgeries (elective colonic resection, gastrectomy) III: Contaminated Open, fresh accidental wounds Operations with major break in sterile techniques Gross spillage from GIT Incision in which acute non-purulent inflammation is encountered Examples of Contaminated Wound Spill during elective GI surgery Perforated gastric ulcer Appendicular perforation Penetrating abdominal trauma Enterotomy during bowel obstruction Human bite Open fracture TYPE OF SURGERY INFECTION RATE WITH PROPHYLAXIS IN % INFECTION RATE WITHOUT PROPHYLAXIS IN % CLEAN(no viscus opened) 1-2 1-2 CLEAN CONTAMINATED (viscus opened, minimal spillage) 3 6-9 CONTAMINATED (open viscus with spillage or inflammatory disease) 6 13-20 DIY (pus/perforation/incision through abscess) 7 40 Table no. 5.4 from Bailey and love's Sho practice of surgery, 27 Ed , Pg no-53
question_upd: What percentage of surgical site infections occur in patients with clean-contaminated wounds after receiving prophylactic antibiotics?
exp_upd:
Wounds can be classified into four categories: clean, clean-contaminated, contaminated, and dirty-infected (D-I-Y). Each category is defined by the level of contamination and the risk of infection.

A clean wound is an uninfected operative wound without inflammation, where no respiratory, alimentary, genital, or infected urinary tract is entered. The wound is closed primarily, if necessary, and may be drained with a closed drain. Examples of clean wounds include inguinal hernia, joint replacement, thyroidectomy, mastectomy, and abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) repair.

A clean-contaminated wound is an operative wound where the respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary tract is entered under controlled conditions without unusual contamination. Examples of clean-contaminated wounds include cholecystectomy, CBD exploration, and elective gastrointestinal surgeries such as elective colonic resection and gastrectomy.

A contaminated wound is an open, fresh accidental wound or an operation with a major break in sterile technique, resulting in gross spillage from the gastrointestinal tract or incision in which acute non-purulent inflammation is encountered. Examples of contaminated wounds include spill during elective gastrointestinal surgery, perforated gastric ulcer, appendicular perforation, penetrating abdominal trauma, enterotomy during bowel obstruction, and human bite. Open fractures also fall into this category.

The infection rate for each category is as follows: clean wounds have an infection rate of 1-2% with prophylaxis and 1-2% without prophylaxis; clean-contaminated wounds have an infection rate of 3% with prophylaxis and 6-9% without prophylaxis; contaminated wounds have an infection rate of 6% with prophylaxis and 13-20% without prophylaxis; and D-I-Y wounds have an infection rate of 7% with prophylaxis and 40% without prophylaxis.

exp_upd: Metoprolol is a beta blocker that can slow the heart rate (HR). Verapamil, on the other hand, is a calcium channel blocker that can cause a delay in the conduction of electrical signals through the atrioventricular (A-V) node. This combination can also increase the risk of torsade de pointes, a type of ventricular tachycardia. Antiarrhythmic medications, such as those in Class IA, IC, and III, are often used to treat this condition.
